## Summary

**What it is:** an eight-point checklist, headed "Nate Silver on how to become a better forecaster — 8 lessons for anyone building sports prediction models". Each lesson has three parts: a one-line principle, a one-to-two-sentence explanation, and a **"For your model:"** line that translates the principle into a modelling practice. Footer, verbatim: "Lessons paraphrased from Nate Silver's writings and interviews, including *Why I Started FiveThirtyEight*, HBR IdeaCast, and Freakonomics. 'For your model' guidance is our own practical application."

The eight lessons (headings verbatim; bodies close-paraphrased from the OCR):

1. **Think in probabilities, not certainties.** Forecasts describe a range of possible outcomes, not a guaranteed result. *For your model:* output win probabilities instead of just picks, and compare them with sportsbook prices.
2. **Check calibration.** If you forecast 60% repeatedly, roughly 6 in 10 comparable outcomes should happen over time. *For your model:* group saved predictions into probability ranges and compare forecasts with actual win rates.
3. **Update when the evidence changes.** A forecast should change when credible new information arrives, such as injuries or lineup changes. *For your model:* save timestamped pregame projections and update them when important inputs change.
4. **Start simple; add complexity carefully.** Silver described starting with a weighted polling average before building a more complicated forecasting model. *For your model:* test against a simple baseline before adding new features; keep only improvements that hold up on unseen data.
5. **Question suspicious patterns.** Data mining can uncover convincing-looking patterns that do not persist. *For your model:* test new variables on games that were not used to develop or tune the model.
6. **Use independent perspectives.** Comparing approaches can expose blind spots, especially when the sources are genuinely independent. *For your model:* benchmark your forecasts against other models and the market, and investigate large disagreements.
7. **Learn from repeated feedback.** Forecasting improves when predictions are made often enough to compare them with observable outcomes. *For your model:* score every frozen prediction, including losses, and examine performance over time.
8. **Respect uncertainty and limitations.** Forecasts depend on assumptions, noisy data and researcher choices. Even strong predictions can be wrong. *For your model:* stress-test fragile assumptions and communicate uncertainty rather than guaranteed picks.

## Why it matters

- **Forecasting hygiene is backtest hygiene with probabilities in place of returns.** Lesson 5 is out-of-sample validation under another name — the same discipline the vault's validation standard rests on ([[2026-10-28-margincall4-overfitting-validation-dsr-pbo-walkforward]]; which checks actually catch overfitting per [[2026-10-31-dmartin-calibrating-robustness-checks]]). Lesson 4 is baseline-first: a weighted polling average is the "simple model to beat", kept only if the gain survives unseen data.
- **Lessons 3 + 7 are the research-log habit.** Timestamped pregame projections written *before* the outcome (3) are what make "score every frozen prediction, including losses" (7) possible at all — without the frozen record, only the memorable calls get scored. That is the hypothesis-before-run / summary-after pattern of [[2026-11-27-systematicpeter-llm-research-workflow-second-brain]], moved from backtests to forecasts.
- **Lesson 2 is calibration stated as a test.** Bin predictions by stated probability, compare with realised frequency. Same check [[2026-10-21-omarsar0-decision-model-evals]] applies to LLM judges ("scores are not probabilities until you check calibration"; Platt scaling as the fix), and the one [[2026-11-27-enjeeneer-mantic-scout-forecasting-agent]] illustrates from the other side: in Mantic's simulation an overconfident forecast beats a calibrated one 60% of the time on single questions yet loses 1.16 nats on average — the reason lesson 7 says score *every* prediction, not the wins.
- **Lessons 1 + 6 make the sportsbook the reference point.** The model's output is a probability; "edge" means disagreement with the price, and lesson 6 says large disagreements are to be *investigated*, not banked. The market is treated as a benchmark to explain, not a foil.
- **Skepticism gates:** (1) **a paraphrase of a paraphrase** — the carousel is the author's summary of Silver's ideas from talks and interviews; nothing is quoted, the three named sources are not linked, and no line here can be checked against Silver's own words from this capture; (2) the "For your model" lines are the author's application, not Silver's — the footer says so; (3) **nothing is quantified** — no evidence offered that following the eight lessons improves any model's results; it is craft advice; (4) sports-betting vocabulary (sportsbook prices, injuries, lineups), but the lessons themselves are domain-agnostic; (5) the five replies were not read.
- **Librarian's reading:** the one lesson that cannot be shortcut is 7 — it needs the log from lesson 3 to exist first. Everything else is standard model hygiene that most forecasters would endorse and fewer practise.
